A.explanation: This uses acceleration alone as force and ignores the $2.5\text{ kg}$ mass in $F = ma$.

B.explanation: This results from using final velocity $12.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ divided by $15.0\text{ s}$, ignoring the $3.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ starting velocity.

C.explanation: Acceleration $0.60\text{ m s}^{-2}$ times mass $2.5\text{ kg}$ gives $1.5\text{ N}$.

D.explanation: This results from using $12.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ divided by $15.0\text{ s}$ as acceleration and then multiplying by $2.5\text{ kg}$.

hints: Notice the line does not start at zero: read the velocity at $0\text{ s}$ as about $3.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ and at $15.0\text{ s}$ as $12.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$.
Recall that the gradient of a velocity-time graph equals acceleration, so you need change in velocity divided by $15.0\text{ s}$.
Recall $F = ma$ for resultant force, so multiply your acceleration by the given mass $2.5\text{ kg}$ and check the unit $\text{N}$.
walkthrough: Read the graph endpoints: initial velocity $v_i = 3.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 0$ and final velocity $v_f = 12.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$ at $t = 15.0\text{ s}$.
State the rule: acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph, $a = \Delta v / \Delta t$.
Calculate the change: $\Delta v = 12.0 - 3.0 = 9.0\text{ m s}^{-1}$, so $a = 9.0 / 15.0 = 0.60\text{ m s}^{-2}$.
Apply Newton's second law for resultant force: $F = ma = 2.5 \times 0.60$.
This gives $F = 1.5\text{ N}$, with correct unit $\text{kg m s}^{-2} = \text{N}$. This is option C.
